qs.q: A 40-year-old male with a history of recurrent flank pain and hematuria develops sudden-onset left-sided varicocele and severe left flank pain. Renal duplex ultrasonography reveals absent flow in the left renal vein. What is the most likely underlying hypercoagulable state contributing to this presentation?
qs.e: Nephrotic syndrome causes urinary loss of antithrombin III, predisposing patients to renal vein thrombosis.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with an acute, right-sided, non-reducing varicocele. What is the most crucial next clinical step?
o: Reassure patient as normal physiological variant.
Aspirate pampiniform plexus to relieve congestion.
Request imaging to investigate retroperitoneal tumour.
qs.e: An acute, right-sided, or non-reducing varicocele suggests an obstructing retroperitoneal or renal tumour such as renal cell carcinoma, necessitating urgent imaging. Routine varicoceles are typically left-sided and decompress when supine.

qs.q: An adolescent male is diagnosed with a varicocele associated with abnormal semen parameters and ipsilateral testicular atrophy. What are the established clinical indications for treating this varicocele?
o: Pain, infertility with abnormal semen, and testicular atrophy
Asymptomatic presentation with normal physical growth parameters
Cosmetic patient preference and uncomplicated transillumination
Acute right-sided swelling with absent inguinal cough impulse
qs.e: Indications for varicocele treatment include pain, infertility with abnormal semen, and testicular atrophy in adolescents. Asymptomatic incidental varicoceles do not routinely require intervention.

qs.q: A 62-year-old man presents with a left-sided varicocele that does not empty when he lies down, alongside macroscopic haematuria. What is the precise mechanism responsible for this physical sign?
o: Direct invasion of the pampiniform plexus by a collecting duct carcinoma
Thrombosis of the inferior vena cava extending to the common iliac vein
Tumour thrombus obstructing the left testicular vein at the renal vein
Direct compression of the left spermatic artery by retroperitoneal nodes
qs.e: An acute left varicocele that does not empty on lying down occurs when a tumour thrombus obstructs the left testicular vein at its entry into the left renal vein. This is a classic local clinical sign of renal cell carcinoma.

ai.summary: A dilated pampiniform plexus caused by incompetent valves, most often on the left. It presents as a gravity‑dependent scrotal swelling and may impair fertility. Diagnosis relies on history, physical exam and, when available, Doppler ultrasound.

sections.p: Varicocele is a tortuous, dilated pampiniform venous plexus of the spermatic cord. It is usually left‑sided due to the angle of the left testicular vein.

t.a: History of scrotal heaviness, pain, or infertility
t.b: Identifies typical symptoms and prompts further assessment

t.a: Physical exam with patient standing and Valsalva
t.b: Positive if a palpable, soft, cord‑like swelling increases with strain
Confirms venous dilation, valve incompetence and excludes other masses

sections.p: The Dubin–Anderson grading system classifies varicoceles from I (palpable only) to III (visible and palpable).
b: Grade III – visible, no need for Valsalva

sections.p: Primary cause is valve incompetence in the pampiniform plexus. Secondary causes include retroperitoneal masses, renal cell carcinoma, or pelvic congestion.
b: Left testicular vein joins left renal vein at right angle

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, a focused history and bedside exam are primary. Ultrasound with Doppler confirms diagnosis and rules out malignancy.

sections.p: Non‑reducing or right‑sided varicocele warrants imaging for malignancy. Untreated varicocele can lead to infertility, testicular atrophy, or pain.
Treat symptomatic or infertile patients with microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy or laparoscopic ligation. Embolisation is an alternative when surgery is unavailable.
b: Microsurgical varicocelectomy – highest success, least recurrence

sections.p: Epididymal cysts, hydrocele, testicular tumour, and inguinal hernia can mimic varicocele.
A normal Doppler may miss a small varicocele; a negative Valsalva does not exclude a grade I lesion.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man reports a dragging ache in the left scrotum that worsens when standing. What is the most appropriate first step? — History of Valsalva, physical exam, and if available, Doppler ultrasound to confirm varicocele.
A patient with a left varicocele presents with sudden right‑sided scrotal swelling. What is the next investigation? — CT abdomen to rule out retroperitoneal tumour.
Why is a left‑sided varicocele more common than right‑sided? — The left testicular vein joins the left renal vein at a right angle, predisposing to valve incompetence.
What is the gold‑standard treatment for a symptomatic grade II varicocele in a low‑resource setting? — Microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy.
A patient with a varicocele is concerned about fertility. What investigation should you order? — Semen analysis to assess sperm count and motility.

Why might a Doppler ultrasound appear normal in a patient with a clinically evident varicocele? — Small or intermittent dilatations may be missed; repeat imaging or a higher‑resolution scan is needed.
